At the train station where my father worked, the lost property office had no clock. This was not because the railway believed that lost things existed outside time. It was because someone had taken the clock down to change the battery and left it on a train.

My father told this story whenever someone asked him the time. I believed it until I was twelve, when I found the clock in a drawer beneath a stack of forms. Its hands stood at twenty past nine. I brought it out to him, pleased with myself in the merciless way of children who have caught an adult lying.

“Ah,” he said. “It came back.”

On school holidays, I sat behind the counter and did my homework. When I finished, my father let me sort the umbrellas. I liked deciding what counted as brown. There was the brown of a dog asleep in sunlight, the brown of tea before milk, and the brown of an umbrella that wanted very badly to be black. On the forms, all of them were BRN.

My father kept the umbrellas in a barrel. Everything else went on shelves, except for a cello, which sat upright in the chair beside the filing cabinet. During a week of heavy rain, my father moved the chair away from a leak in the ceiling. He moved my homework, too, but only after I asked.

Some people turned up so sure of what they had lost that they were unable to recognize it. A man once insisted that his briefcase had a brass clasp. My father set a briefcase with a silver clasp on the counter. The man shook his head. My father opened it and turned it around. Inside were three oranges and a photograph of the man standing beside a horse.

“That’s my horse,” the man said, still doubtful.

Other people remembered things no one could check. A woman looking for a red scarf said it smelled of her sister’s kitchen. My father brought out two red scarves and left her alone with them. She smelled the first one, then the second, then the first again. In the end she went away without either. My father folded them and put them back. One was a little damp where she had held it to her face.

The cello stayed for nine months. I asked how anyone could forget a cello, and my father said the trick was to carry it every day. Carry a cello once and it takes up your whole mind. Carry one for twenty years and you can get off a train thinking about whether you need potatoes.

This explanation pleased me so much that I tried to forget my schoolbag. I thought about potatoes all the way home. When I got there, I still had the bag, but I had left my coat on the train. My father made me fill in a form.

Years later, when the station was being renovated, the railway moved lost property to a warehouse at the end of a bus route. My father was offered a job there. He went out to look at it and found a bright room with a barcode reader. There would be no counter. People would describe their things online and, if there was a match, pay to have them posted.

“They’ll get more back this way,” he told me.

He meant it. He retired anyway.

On his last Saturday I helped him empty the office. The cellar smell I had always attributed to the building turned out to belong to the umbrella barrel. We carried it onto the platform. In the sunshine, I could see that the wood was stained purple in places. My father said it had come from a pub. I had the sudden, childish feeling that he ought to have told me this before.

At the back of a shelf we found a biscuit tin full of single gloves. My father tipped them out and began trying to make pairs. I reminded him that the warehouse van was due at eleven.

“I know,” he said, slipping a small blue glove over two fingers.

He found another blue one, a little larger, with a different pattern at the wrist. He laid them side by side. They were both left hands.

While he looked through the pile again, I opened the drawer and took out the clock. There was no battery in it. I asked him why he had kept it all those years.

“Somebody might want it,” he said.

“Who? It belongs to the railway.”

He took it from me and turned it over. On the back, written in nail polish, was a name I recognized as my mother’s. She had worked in the station café before I was born. She used to put her name on everything she brought to work because the café manager had the same taste in crockery.

“She loaned it to me,” my father said. “I kept meaning to get her another one.”

My mother was alive and living twenty minutes away. She and my father had been divorced for sixteen years. I called her from the platform and asked if she remembered the clock.

“Of course,” she said. “Does it still gain seven minutes a day?”

I looked through the office window at my father. He had found two gloves that might have been a pair. He laid one on top of the other, checking the thumbs.

“I don’t know,” I told her. “Do you want it back?”

There was a pause. I could hear a cupboard opening and the clink of a cup being set down.

“No,” she said. “But tell him I want my biscuit tin.”

I went back inside and picked up the lid. It was blue, with a picture of a yacht leaning into the wind. My father looked at it for a moment, then swept the gloves into a cardboard box for the warehouse. He wiped the tin with the sleeve of his shirt and pressed the lid down all the way around.

“You can take that to her,” he said.

“You could take it yourself.”

He pulled his coat off the back of the chair. “I suppose I could.”
